subject: World History
title: Japan's late industrialisation
demand: Compare state direction, imported technology, skills and timing with the West.
route: Open with the latecomer advantage and the sovereignty threat. Compare state coordination, technology borrowing, education and private business. Qualify: Britain also used state power and Japan had social costs. End with adapted modernisation rather than a copied model.

subject: World History
title: European rivalry and Africa's artificial states
demand: Explain externally imposed boundaries and assess consequences.
route: Start with the scramble, then connect rivalry to conquest and imposed jurisdictions. Use Berlin accurately: it set claim rules, not every border. Show divided communities, extraction and difficult state-building. Add African resistance and explain why later institutions also matter.

subject: World History
title: American revolt against mercantilism
demand: Substantiate the economic claim through mechanisms.
route: Define mercantilism in one line. Explain trade restrictions, taxation, commercial interests and boycotts. Connect these to representation and the right to govern. Conclude that an economic revolt acquired a wider constitutional meaning; do not narrate every battle.

subject: World History
title: Policies used against the Depression
demand: Identify policy instruments and the problem each addressed.
route: Arrange the answer as problem and instrument: panic and bank stabilisation; weak demand and relief or public works; fragility and regulation; insecurity and social protection. Add monetary expansion and contrast harmful protectionism. State that recovery was uneven and policies varied by country.

subject: World History
title: Lenin's NEP and India's early policies
demand: Evaluate similarities without assuming complete direct copying.
route: Explain NEP as limited markets under state control of major sectors. Identify comparable space for private enterprise and public leadership in India. Then distinguish democratic institutions, the development context and diverse influences on Indian planning. Similar instruments do not prove identical models or a single line of influence.

subject: World History
title: Suez events and Britain's global status
demand: Give the causal sequence, then evaluate the change in power.
route: Use a short sequence: Aswan financing dispute, canal nationalisation, coordinated invasion, international and financial pressure, withdrawal. Spend the remaining space explaining the gap between military force and independent strategic power. Qualify 'final blow': a decisive symbol of decline, not the disappearance of British influence.

subject: World History
title: World developments motivating India's freedom struggle
demand: Link specific global developments to specific Indian responses.
route: Group by political ideas, economic criticism and international examples. Connect rights to equality claims, Japan's 1905 victory to confidence, the Russian Revolution to socialist currents, and world wars to imperial weakness and mobilisation. Show Indian adaptation and domestic agency; avoid a disconnected list of foreign events.

subject: World History
title: Why Britain industrialised first; living conditions; India comparison
demand: Answer all three parts in proportion.
route: Use roughly half the body for the combination of markets, finance, energy, skills and institutions. Cover work, housing, sanitation and inequality next. Compare with India through informal work and migrant conditions, while recognising modern rights and public institutions. Do not equate different historical settings.

subject: World History
title: Germany's responsibility for both world wars
demand: Assess each war separately, then compare the degree of responsibility.
route: For 1914 explain German backing, strategy and escalation, alongside Austrian, Russian and wider rivalries. For 1939 emphasise deliberate Nazi conquest and racial empire; recognise appeasement and other aggressive powers as context. Your judgment should state why German responsibility was greater and clearer in the second war.

subject: World History
title: Educated African elites and West African liberation
demand: Examine leadership and qualify with popular participation.
route: Explain education, legal vocabulary, journalism and Pan-African networks. Use Nkrumah and Azikiwe for distinct examples. Then show that parties needed workers, farmers, women traders and other groups. Conclude that elites supplied important leadership within wider social struggles.

subject: World History
title: Problems during Malayan decolonisation
demand: Identify the particular obstacles, not generic colonialism alone.
route: Use four headings: citizenship and representation; ethnic and constitutional bargaining; communist insurgency and Emergency; rubber, tin and British strategic interests. Explain how the problems interacted. End with independence in 1957 while the Emergency continued to 1960. Keep Malaysia's later formation separate.

subject: World History
title: Indian indenture and cultural identity overseas [overlap]
demand: Cover both labour demand and cultural continuity through adaptation.
route: First explain post-slavery plantation demand, Indian rural distress, recruitment and coercive contracts. Then show religious practice, festivals, food, language and community institutions in destinations such as Mauritius and Trinidad. Include cultural mixing and changing identities. This is also a society and diaspora question, not only world history.

subject: World History
title: American and French revolutions as modern foundations
demand: Compare political contributions and acknowledge exclusions.
route: Organise by sovereignty, rights, constitutionalism, equality and national identity. Link American federal institutions with the French attack on inherited privilege. Explain international diffusion and adaptation. Use slavery and women's exclusion to show incomplete promises; avoid two separate chronological essays.

subject: World History
title: Interwar threats to the democratic state
demand: Evaluate the scale, causes, mechanisms and limits of the threat.
route: Begin with fragile post-war legitimacy. Explain social conflict, economic crises, fascist organisation, elite accommodation and emergency powers. Use Italy and Germany precisely. Add the survival and adaptation of some democracies so the judgment is evaluated rather than universalised.

subject: World History
title: Railways' social and economic effects across countries
demand: Compare countries, effects and distribution.
route: Use Britain for industrial linkages, the United States for continental markets and dispossession, and India for colonial exports plus mobility and political contact. Cover employment, migration and social exchange alongside economic integration. Conclude that institutions and ownership shaped gains.

subject: World History
title: First World War and the balance of power
demand: Test how far the explanation works, including its limits.
route: Explain the German power shift and the security calculations of Britain, France, Russia and Austria-Hungary. Then add revisionist ambitions, nationalism, empire and July decisions. Distinguish preserving a balance from seeking to change it. Conclude that balance of power is a framework, not a complete single cause.

subject: World History
title: British industrialisation and Indian craft decline
demand: Assess machinery together with colonial policy and uneven outcomes.
route: Explain productivity and price competition first. Then add trade asymmetry, political subordination, lost patronage and changing demand. Use railways as an amplifier of market penetration. Mention survival and adaptation of handlooms. Conclude that industrial superiority worked through colonial institutions rather than technology acting alone.

subject: World History
title: French Revolution's continuing relevance
demand: Translate its principles into enduring questions and qualify the legacy.
route: Use sovereignty, legal equality, liberty, civic nationhood and resistance to privilege. Explain each connection rather than adding modern slogans. Add women's exclusion, slavery and the Terror. Conclude that the revolution supplied standards by which later societies could judge its own failures as well as other injustices.
